title: Capcom's Notification of "CAPCOM ID Unauthorized Access" Received, but Isn't Their Security Configuration Way Too Lax?
description: Capcom notified customers of unauthorized access to CAPCOM ID accounts but their email security configuration is weak. Their official notification emails failed DMARC alignment checks despite passing SPF and DKIM individually. Capcom's DMARC policy is set to 'p=none', which only monitors failures without requesting rejection or quarantine of unauthenticated emails. This lax configuration increases the risk of phishing and spoofing attacks impersonating Capcom. The company uses an external email delivery service but has not properly aligned authentication to prevent spoofing. The notification warns customers about potential misuse of their information but Capcom has not taken stronger email security measures to prevent secondary damage.

aiSummary: Capcom sent a data breach notification regarding unauthorized access to CAPCOM ID accounts. The notification emails failed DMARC alignment checks because the SPF and DKIM authentication did not align with the capcom.com domain in the From header. Capcom's SPF record ends with a softfail (~all), and their DMARC policy is set to 'p=none', meaning no enforcement action is requested on failed authentication. This configuration allows potentially spoofed emails to be delivered, increasing phishing risks. Capcom uses an external email delivery service that is not properly configured for domain alignment, contributing to DMARC failures. Despite warning customers about possible fraudulent emails, Capcom has not updated its email authentication policies to quarantine or reject unauthenticated messages, leaving users exposed to secondary attacks.
aiImpact: The weak DMARC policy and misaligned email authentication increase the risk that attackers can send spoofed emails appearing to come from Capcom. This can facilitate phishing attacks and fraud targeting affected customers. The notification emails themselves failed DMARC alignment, which may reduce trust in official communications. Without enforcement of DMARC policies, recipients' mail servers may deliver spoofed or fraudulent emails, potentially leading to further compromise or data misuse.
